active_puzzle.opening: I am a student studying in the University of Hong Kong. I must choose my courses before the deadline. All of my courses were gone in one evening. What happened?
active_puzzle.reference_answer: I needed to attend a mandatory high table dinner and was asked to indicate which courses I prefer to eat before the deadline. In the evening when I attended the high table dinner, I arrived punctually. I did not finish every course in my three-course meal because I don't like its taste. Therefore I asked the waiter to collect the remains each time he serves the next course and thus my courses are eventually gone.

Therefore I asked the waiter to collect the remains each time he serves the next course and thus my courses are eventually gone.

The narrator completes the project poorly under that workload.
The poor project grade contributes heavily to the final grade and causes failure despite the narrator’s general academic strength.
label_boundaries: Other people contributed causally through free-riding. Do not recast their inaction as an independent administrative decision or a board overriding results. Questions asserting that alternative cause are no.

A requirement other than examinations exists (the group project): yes. A question saying the narrator did NOT COMPLETE it is no, because it was completed poorly. A no to the latter never denies the existence of project work.
Specific exams in this failed course or scores on them are unspecified, matching the existing human irrelevant labels. Strong exam ability in general is stated in the opening.

When a player asks for the decision-maker after a mistaken administrative-decision premise, reject that proposed causal story. Ordinary marking of poor work is not a newly invented arbitrary decision. Do not name a hidden administrator or professor to preserve earlier feedback.

host_examples.question: Was the decision-maker a teacher or professor after all, rather than an administrator/committee?

public_history.text: The student was officially enrolled in the course and passed all its tests and exams. However, they were not allowed to receive a passing grade in that enrolled course because an administrator or committee — not the instructor, and acting on a school policy or eligibility rule rather than on the student's coursework — made the decision that caused the fail. The passing work did not translate into credit for the enrolled course, so despite performing brilliantly, the student received a failing grade.

Did the administrator or committee fail the student because the student was taking the course via a program (such as a foreign exchange, visiting, or transfer program) that the committee ruled could not grant credit toward the student's degree?

Did the student's portion contain a narrow technical error such that, if only that error were absent, the project would still fail for an unrelated reason?
